subject: Food Science
title: Spice Trade and Food Science
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Spice Trade and Food Science.

hook.text: In the 1400s, a pound of nutmeg was worth more than a cow. The spice trade drove exploration, colonization, and global conflict.

buildup.text: Spices weren't flavor—they masked off-tastes in aging food, provided antimicrobial protection, and served as medicine before.

discovery.text: A 1998 Cornell study proved that spice use correlates with climate: hotter countries use more antimicrobial spices because food.

twist.text: Columbus didn't find India—but he found chili peppers.

climax.text: The spice trade created the first global supply chains. The Dutch East India Company (1602) was history's first multinational.

punchline.text: Spices preserved food, funded empires, and launched globalization.

quiz.question: Why do hotter countries tend to use more spices in cooking?
options: Food spoils faster in heat—antimicrobial spices helped preserve it before refrigeration
